extracted.intended_audience: students, educators, and writers researching narrative technique and literary devices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for identifying, employing, and analysing unreliable narrators in fiction and visual media; covers definition, types (intentional vs unintentional), functions, modes of revelation, and canonical examples. Useful for literary analysis and creative-writing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of credibility regarding plot events
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator is defined by their lack of credibility about plot events—telling lies, omitting or misrepresenting important information, or presenting inaccurate interpretations as objective truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This unreliability may be immediately apparent or may surface gradually as contradictions emerge; it includes intentional deception, omission, misrepresentation, and sincere but mistaken interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective (typically first-person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narrators are usually features of literary works written in the first person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While most commonly first-person, the device can appear in other narrative modes and also in visual media (film and television). Consider how point of view limits or frames the narrator's knowledge and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and manner of revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliability can be immediately obvious to the reader or revealed gradually as additional information contradicts earlier statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the author staggers information, plants contradictions, or withholds facts to produce either early suspicion or a later twist; the method of revelation shapes reader experience and interpretive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional vs. unintentional unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narrators can be divided into unintentionally unreliable narrators and intentionally unreliable narrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unintentional unreliability often stems from the narrator's age, lack of experience or understanding, or outsider status; it challenges readers to critique the narrator's worldview. Intentional unreliability involves deliberate deception or concealment for secret or sinister reasons (e.g., Humbert Humbert in Lolita).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and psychological motives for unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator unreliability may originate from motives such as guilt, insanity, self-deception, or conscious deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or analyzing such narrators, consider psychological state and motives (e.g., guilt in Humbert Humbert; insanity in The Tell-Tale Heart) and how these shape distortions of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary functions: exploring fallibility of perception and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary fiction, unreliable narrators are often used to examine or reflect the fallibility of human perception and memory and to serve thematic, philosophical, or metacommentary purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how unreliability advances themes, deepens ambiguity, or provokes interpretive engagement rather than simply serving plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre function: misdirection and plot twists in popular fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular fiction—particularly mystery, suspense, and crime stories—unreliable narrators are frequently used to misdirect readers and create effective twists that overturn expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how unreliability is used instrumentally to shape reader assumptions and the timing of revelations (e.g., The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, Gone Girl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of authorial subjectivity and reader expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Wayne Booth's formulation emphasizes authorial subjectivity and the engagement between author, work, and reader; unreliable narration arises from this interplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider authorial stance and how the text solicits or manipulates reader expectations—unreliable narration can be a deliberate authorial strategy to foreground subjectivity and reader response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across media
rubrics_metrics.description: While primarily associated with prose fiction, unreliable narration also appears in cinema and television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or writing for film/TV, adapt the device to visual/structural techniques (multiple perspectives, editing, voiceover) as in Rashomon, Memento, or Mr. Robot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of canonical examples as reference models
rubrics_metrics.description: Several classic and contemporary works exemplify unreliable narration and serve as models for study: Gulliver's Travels; Wuthering Heights; Lolita; The Tell‑Tale Heart; The Murder of Roger Ackroyd; The Wasp Factory; Fight Club; The Girl on the Train; films like Rashomon, Memento, Shutter Island.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study these examples to see different strategies (psychological distortion, deliberate deception, structural misdirection) and their effects on theme and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging critical reader engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narrators often encourage readers to read critically, interrogate the narrator's account, and piece together a more objective or alternative understanding of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the text scaffolds reader skepticism—through contradictions, external evidence, or other characters' perspectives—and how this shapes interpretive labor.
